'''James Edward Zimmerman''' (February 19, 1923 &ndash; August 4, 1999) was a [https://spectrum.ieee.org/how-the-ford-motor-co-invented-the-squid coinventor] of the radio-frequency [[superconducting]] [[quantum]] interference device ([[SQUID]]).<ref name=":0">{{Cite journal |last1=Kautz |first1=Richard L. |last2=Sullivan |first2=Donald B. |date=July 2007 |title=James Edward Zimmerman |journal=[[Physics Today]] |volume=53 |issue=7 |pages=70–71 |doi=10.1063/1.1292491}}</ref><ref name=":1">{{Cite journal |last=Kautz |first=Richard L. |date=2001-03-01 |title=Jim Zimmerman and the SQUID |url=https://www.nist.gov/publications/jim-zimmerman-and-squid |journal= IEEE Transactions on Applied Superconductivity|language=en |volume=11 |issue=1 |pages=1026–1031 |doi=10.1109/77.919524 |bibcode=2001ITAS...11.1026K |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250324023639/https://www.nist.gov/publications/jim-zimmerman-and-squid |archive-date=2025-03-24}}</ref>

== Early life and education ==
Zimmerman was born in [[Lantry, South Dakota]] and grew up on a ranch. He received a [[Bachelor of Science|B.S.]] in [[electrical engineering]] from the [[South Dakota School of Mines and Technology]] in 1943.<ref name=":0" /> Afterward, he joined the Westinghouse Research Laboratory in [[Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania]]. He received a [[Doctor of Philosophy|Ph.D.]] in [[physics]] from the [[Carnegie Institute of Technology]] in 1953.<ref name=":0" />

== Career ==
From 1953 to 1955, Zimmerman worked for the [[Smithsonian Institution]] and moved to California to work at the [[Table Mountain Observatory]]. <ref name=":1" /> 

In 1955, Zimmerman began working at the [[Ford Motor Company]] in Dearborn, Michigan. He co-invented the SQUID while working at Ford in 1965, and the term "SQUID" was coined in 1966.<ref name=":1" /> Zimmerman left Dearborn in 1967 due to disagreements with SQUID collaborator James Mercereau. He joined [[Aeronutronic]], a defense division of [[Philco-Ford]].

In 1970, Zimmerman joined the [[National Bureau of Standards]], where he worked until 1985. While at NIST, Zimmerman introduced two important innovations in SQUID magnetometry:
* Fractional-turn SQUID, improving the coupling efficiency
* SQUID gradiometer, improving sensitivity to nearby fields

In addition, in the late 1970s and early 1980s, he also contributed to the development of low-power closed-cycle [[Stirling engine|Stirling refrigerators]], to reach temperatures in the range 4K - 8K with the purpose of cooling SQUID devices and small-scale [[Technological applications of superconductivity|superconducting electronics]] without resorting to [[liquid helium]] [[Vacuum flask|dewar]] vessels. <ref name=":1" /> 

A major achievement was the use of plastic parts made in the laboratory, which would be assembled in a totally non-magnetic [[cryocooler]] (refrigerator), in order not to interfere with highly sensitive SQUIDs.
Later, he was also involved in the development of [[pulse tube cryocooler]]s.

== Personal life ==
Zimmerman married Australian citizen Jean McLeod, whom he met while in Sydney for a Westinghouse Research Laboratory assignment. They had one daughter, Janet, born in 1947.<ref name=":1" /> 

Zimmerman died of cancer on August 4, 1999.

== Awards ==
*NIST Fellow
*[[Samuel Wesley Stratton Award]], the highest award for scientific achievement conferred by NIST
